title: The soul's self-harm
hook: the soul harms itself most when it turns against others in anger (Meditations 2.16)

segments.voice: Yesterday: no prying, and affection instead. Your line was not my business. What did you leave alone? Day five hundred thirty-eight.

There's an old saying, often repeated and of uncertain origin, that holding a grudge is like drinking poison and waiting for the other person to get sick. Marcus never heard it, but his notebook circles the same idea. In section sixteen he lists the ways a soul wounds itself, and one of them is anger. A word first: Marcus means this as a picture of what anger and falseness do inside us. If the phrase self-harm touches something painful in your own life, please reach out to someone you trust today. Now, the entry. The soul's self-harm.
screen: `DRINKING THE POISON YOURSELF.` → `A LIST OF INNER WOUNDS.` → `THE SOUL'S SELF-HARM.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. The soul does violence to itself, Marcus says, and he names five ways. The striking thing is the direction. We usually think of harm as something done to us. Marcus is interested in the harm we do from the inside. Second, a growth on the world. The first way is when the soul becomes, in his image, like a swelling or a tumor on the universe: when it rages against whatever happens, as if it could pull away from the whole of nature it belongs to. Third, turning against others. The second way is today's center: when the soul turns away from another person, or moves against them meaning to hurt them, the way angry people do. Marcus's point is that anger at someone else wounds the one who carries it. We were made, he said earlier in this book, to work together, like two hands. A hand that strikes the other hand hurts the body it belongs to. Fourth, masks and aimlessness. The other ways: when the soul is overpowered by pleasure or pain; when it plays a part, saying or doing anything false; and when it acts with no aim at all, carelessly, without thinking. Notice that all five are harms done from inside. And notice how practical that is. If the harm comes from inside, so can the repair. A grudge softened by one degree is one less wound. Don't harm myself is a surprisingly kind way to say: let it go a little.
screen: `FIVE WAYS THE SOUL HURTS ITSELF.` · `RAGING LIKE A GROWTH ON THE WORLD.` · `TURNING AGAINST OTHERS IN ANGER.` · `PLEASURE, MASKS, AND NO AIM.` · then, large: `DON'T HARM MYSELF.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one grudge you're carrying. Not the biggest. A medium one. Picture the person. Notice where the grudge lives in your body: jaw, chest, stomach. Now, without excusing anything they did, breathe into that place and let it soften by one degree. Just one. You're not doing this for them. You're putting down a little of what you've been carrying. The bell holds the time.
Tumor. Marcus's image for a soul that rages against what happens, as if it could pull away from the whole of nature it belongs to. Today's word.
Your line: don't harm myself. When a grudge flares today, remember who it's really hurting, and soften it, even slightly. Day five hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism treat anger and resentment as harms to their own character first, and work to loosen grudges for that reason.

fork.setup: someone wronged you months ago. you still replay it daily. what does Meditations 2.16 suggest about who's being hurt?
options: you: turning against someone in anger wounds your own soul.
fork.reveal: Marcus lists turning against another in anger as a way the soul does violence to itself.

trapdoor: what you thought: anger is bad manners.
what it means: anger, falseness and aimlessness are wounds the soul gives itself, and so the soul can begin its own repair.
what a scholar hears: the image of the soul as a growth on the cosmos reflects the Stoic view of each person as a part of one living whole.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): anger is the second of five self-harms in 2.16, not "the one at the center" or "chief among them"; removed the spoken reference to "the outline"; cut the unsupported "four of the five are things we choose" and the "deepest harm" superlative; "People... often" to "Some people" in howItsDone.

Meditations 2.16 paraphrased: the soul does violence to itself when it becomes an abscess or tumor on the universe (vexed at what happens); when it turns away from any man or moves toward him intending injury, as the angry do; when overpowered by pleasure or pain; when it plays a part and does or says anything insincerely; when it allows any act to be without aim. Confirm the count (five) and order.
The grudge/poison saying is introduced as 'of uncertain origin' (it is often misattributed to the Buddha and others). Confirm hedge.
